title: Function interface validator and cross-SDK call pattern book
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description: Goal: Provide a concise, language-appropriate validator and a set of ergonomic invocation helpers for Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs that make function/tool calling robust, auditable, and straightforward to integrate in production workloads. This ticket covers the design for: (1) a deterministic schema compatibility check (fingerprint + semantic diff), (2) runtime validation with permissive coercions for common types, (3) a lightweight client-side sandbox for malformed outputs, (4) streaming-friendly invocation helpers that support resumable streams and idempotency, and (5) shared examples and migration guidance for existing customers.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Library implements schema fingerprinting and a compatibility API: isCompatible(protoA, protoB) -> (compatible|minor|breaking). 2) Python/TS/Go validators each expose validate(schema, payload, options) returning normalized payload and a list of non-fatal warnings. 3) Streaming helper supports resume tokens and optional at-least-once vs exactly-once semantics with idempotency-key wiring. 4) Retry policy helpers (exponential/backoff-with-jitter) pluggable per-language and documented with examples. 5) Unit + integration tests demonstrating recovery from partial stream failure and cross-language contract mismatch detection.
design_notes: - Use a compact schema fingerprint (Blake3 truncated) to allow cheap compatibility checks in telemetry and cache keys. - Validation should be layered: quick structural check (fast-path), then optional deep coercion (strings->numbers/dates) controlled by flags. - For streaming, embed a small per-message header that can carry a resume cursor and a checksum. This requires coordination with runtime to preserve session affinity or to accept stateless resume tokens. - Favor explicit idempotency keys for calls that can mutate downstream state. - Keep client helpers thin: they should orchestrate retries/stream resume but surface raw stream fragments for apps that want custom assembly.
tradeoffs: - Deep coercion improves UX but risks hiding model regressions; we will default to conservative coercion and log warnings. - Adding per-message headers to streaming payloads increases wire protocol complexity; alternative is to encode resume info within the ephemeral KV cache, but that hurts cross-process resume. - Implementing exactly-once semantics end-to-end is expensive; initial scope provides at-least-once with idempotency primitives and guidance for customers needing stronger guarantees.
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (2 wks): prototype schema fingerprint and compatibility checker; add unit tests and a small CLI for diffing two schemas. Phase 2 (3 wks): implement validators in Python and TypeScript with permissive coercion flags and warnings; publish preview. Phase 3 (2 wks): Go validator + streaming helper prototypes that support resume tokens and idempotency. Phase 4 (1 wk): examples, migration guide, integration tests, and rollout plan (canary SDK release + feature flag on runtime).
risks: - Backwards compatibility: older clients without resume token support may fail to reattach to ongoing streams. - Telemetry noise from coercion warnings could be high if models change output shapes frequently. - Cross-lang differences in numeric/date handling could cause subtle mismatch; we will add conformance tests.
testing_plan: - Conformance matrix: Python <-> Runtime, TypeScript <-> Runtime, Go <-> Runtime. - Simulate: truncated stream, network interruption, mis-typed fields (e.g., id as string vs number), and incompatible schema changes. - Property tests for fingerprint idempotence and comparator stability. - Load test: repeated schema-diff checks to ensure fingerprinting is cheap under 1000 req/s.
rollout_and_migration: 1) Release validators as experimental in minor SDK release behind feature flag. 2) Provide a CLI tool for customers to pre-check their registered function schemas against deployed runtime models. 3) Document recommended settings (coercion=false for high-safety customers, coercion=true for rapid PLG onboarding). 4) Collect telemetry for warning rates and server-side deprecation notices before tightening defaults.
